title: Foxconn confirms new OpenAI tie-up in the works
subtitle: Chairman Young Liu said he met Sam Altman to extend their AI-hardware partnership and told reporters there is no AI bubble.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 30, Foxconn Chairman Young Liu told reporters the company is working on a new tie-up with OpenAI and said a joint announcement will follow once details are finalized. Liu confirmed he met OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and framed the new agreement as an extension of a prior deal under which Foxconn designs and engineers AI data-center racks and related hardware. He also pushed back on the dominant market narrative of the week, saying bluntly there is no AI bubble.

Foxconn already runs six factory buildings in Houston producing AI servers for Nvidia, and Liu said the operation needs further expansion to keep up. The company has also deployed more than ten humanoid robots at its Texas facilities for internal use. A separate $71.9 million investment announced in July 2026 funds a Houston AI-server facility supporting Apple production, with construction set to complete in early 2027. Together these moves make Foxconn the quietest but largest beneficiary of the US AI data-center buildout — every hyperscaler eventually orders racks, and most of those racks are assembled by Foxconn.

An expanded OpenAI partnership would plug Foxconn directly into the Stargate buildout, where OpenAI is spending into the hundreds of billions on compute. Foxconn is already reported to have secured exclusive rack orders for the US Stargate project in earlier coverage. For Liu to volunteer that there is no AI bubble is unusual — contract manufacturers normally stay out of valuation debates — and it signals confidence that order books extend well into 2027 and beyond, which is the only data point that matters to a company that lives and dies on multi-year capacity planning.

A takeaway for learners: the AI story most people read is about models and chatbots, but the money and the physical bottleneck is in racks, cooling, interconnects, and the people who screw them together. Foxconn is the single biggest tell on whether frontier labs' infrastructure plans are real: if their order book keeps growing, the buildout is happening. For students and engineers, following the manufacturing supply chain — ODMs, HBM suppliers, substrate makers, power equipment vendors — is one of the most reliable ways to spot which AI narratives have money behind them and which are talk.
